newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: E.Asia Grains - Trade doubts wheat sale to N.Korea.
newsitem.headline: E.Asia Grains - Trade doubts wheat sale to N.Korea.

text.p: South Korean wheat dealers on Monday scoffed at rumours in the U.S. that Cargill sold at least one million tonnes of optional origin wheat to North Korea.
They said Pyongyang had neither the cash nor the infrastructure to handle such a huge quantity of the wheat. Cargill has declined to comment on the rumour.
"I do not believe the rumour that the North bought at least one million tonnes of wheat," a trader with a major flour milling company in Korea said.
"Even though they bought this amount of wheat, where are they going to store it and how (do they) pay it. As far as we know, the North has not enough storage facility and cash," the trader said.
North Korea has been hit hard by several years of crop failures which have left its people on the brink of starvation.

A dealer said two local flour millers, Cheiljedang Corp and Dongah Flour Mills Co Ltd, were expected to jointly re-invite tenders to buy 22,000 tonnes of U.S. wheat for July shipment after passing on last Friday's tenders due to high prices.
The rest of the East Asian grains market was quiet, except for Japanese importers who continue to buy U.S. corn for third quarter shipment.
"We'll continue to cover U.S. corn this week. The weaker freight cost partly encouraged end-users to buy," a corn trader at a major trade house in Tokyo said.
Japan's corn premiums were seen at around 93 U.S. cents a bushel over CBOT July futures.
Chinese exporters were still offering corn to Japan, but there was little interest here as their prices were said to be at a premium over the U.S. crop, traders said.

Corn buyers in South Korea, however, sat it out of the market on expectations that prices would ease further due to reports of good growing weather in the U.S., traders said. Buyers were also well covered up to the end of September.
"We are not expecting any corn purchase order from clients this week," an agent of a foreign grain supplier in Korea said.
Freight rates on the U.S. Gulf/Japan route was quoted at slightly below US$21 per tonne, traders said.
An official with Pan Ocean Shipping Co Ltd in Korea said freight rates from the U.S. Pacific Northwest were steady at $12 a tonne for nearby shipments of Panamax-sized cargoes.
Rates for nearby shipment of Panamax-sized ships from the U.S. Gulf were unchanged at $22 a tonne.
